content: Phosphoserine aminotransferase 1 (PSAT1), also referred to as phosphohydroxythreonine aminotransferase (PSAT), is an enzyme in humans encoded by the PSAT1 gene. The protein produced by this gene is believed to function as a phosphoserine aminotransferase, based on its similarity to homologous proteins found in species such as mice, rabbits, and Drosophila. Alternative splicing of the PSAT1 gene results in the production of two transcript variants, which encode distinct isoforms of the protein. Homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the PSAT1 gene are associated with the development of Neu-Laxova syndrome and phosphoserine aminotransferase deficiency, both of which are severe genetic disorders. Model organisms have been utilized to investigate the functional role of PSAT1. A conditional knockout mouse line, designated Psat1tm1a(KOMP)Wtsi, was created as part of the International Knockout Mouse Consortium program. This initiative is a high-throughput mutagenesis project aimed at generating and distributing animal models of human diseases to researchers worldwide. Male and female mice from this line underwent a standardized phenotypic screening process to assess the effects of PSAT1 gene deletion. In total, 24 tests were conducted on the mutant mice, and two significant abnormalities were identified. No homozygous mutant embryos were detected during gestation, and none survived to the weaning stage. The remaining tests were performed on heterozygous mutant adult mice, and no additional significant abnormalities were observed in these animals.
